title: 3.5 Hypothesis Testing
text:
You arrive here from Effects, so you can already express how big an effect is and you know that results from a sample are never perfectly precise. Here you’ll learn how to derive a testable hypothesis from a theory, and the logic that turns an uncertain sample result into a yes/no decision — the null hypothesis, the p-value, and the confidence interval — which is the reasoning every test in the rest of the book relies on.
→ See this module in the skill tree

title: 3.5 Hypothesis Testing
text:
3.5.1 Deriving hypotheses from theories
In order to use statistical methods to test theories, we first need to derive hypotheses from them. A hypothesis is a testable statement, that when tested empirically provides evidence for or against the theory.
For example, consider the theory that playing violent video games leads to increased aggression in children. There is much disagreement about whether this theory is correct (Griffiths 1999), so it’s important to test it empirically. In order to do so, we need to derive hypotheses that we can conduct to rigorous statistical tests. Some examples of hypotheses are:

There is a relation “between arcade game use and teachers’ ratings of impulsiveness and aggresiveness”. (Lin and Lepper 1987, 81)
Playing violent video games leads to higher levels of heart rate and blood pressure compared to playing non-violent video games. (Lynch 1994)
There will be a “linear increase in aggressive affect after playing nonaggressive, moderately aggresive, and highly aggressive games”. (Scott 1995, 125)

Notice that these hypotheses are more specific than the theory they are derived from. Where the theory talks about concepts, the hypotheses talk about specific relations between variables. Sometimes these variables are only proxies for the concepts in the theory, such as “heart rate” and “blood pressure” are proxies for “aggression”. To provide evidence for causal mechanisms in theories, hypotheses can formulate relations between variables in such a way that a causal order is implied (e.g., increase “after playing”; hearth rate being unlikely to be a cause of playing video games).

Evidence \(\neq\) proof
If an hypothesis is confirmed, it provides evidence in support of the theory. However, note that it does not necessarily prove the theory.
For example, if we find that children who play violent video games are more aggressive, it does not yet prove that the games caused the aggression, because there are other possible explanations for finding this relation. Perhaps people who are already aggressive are more likely to play violent video games, or there could be a confounding variable that causes both aggression and video game playing (e.g., gender, socioeconomic status, or parental involvement). To build stronger evidence, we therefore need to design our studies in such a way that we can rule out these alternative explanations, for instanced by conducting randomized controlled trials, or by statistically controlling for confounders Also see the tutorial on causality. And more generally speaking, a theory is not proven by a single empirical test. Sometimes results only occur in a specific context or sample, or are sheer coincidence. Studies therefore need to be replicated in other contexts or samples to gradually build a stronger case for a theory.
Hypotheses are thus the bridge between theory and statistical methods, and are essential for conducting rigorous research in communication science. They need to be specific enough to be testable, but close enough to the theory they are derived from to allow for meaningful conclusions.

title: 3.5 Hypothesis Testing
section: 3.5.2 The null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis
text:
3.5.2 The null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis
Once we have a hypothesis, such as “playing violent video games leads to a higher heart rate than playing non-violent video games”, we need a way to actually test it against data. Null hypothesis testing does this in a slightly indirect way: instead of trying to directly prove our hypothesis, we formulate its opposite, and then ask whether the data gives us enough reason to reject that opposite.

The null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) is the “nothing is going on” statement: there is no difference between the violent and non-violent game groups in the population. Any difference we see in our sample is purely due to chance (sampling variability, as you saw in Probability & Sampling).
The alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)) is usually the hypothesis we actually derived from theory: there is a real difference in heart rate between the two groups in the population.

We never get to directly observe the population, so we can’t simply check which of the two is true. Instead, the logic works like this: assume the null hypothesis is true, and then ask how likely it would be to see a sample result as extreme as the one we actually observed, just by chance. If that would be very unlikely, we take it as evidence against \(H_0\), and in favor of \(H_1\). If a result like ours would be quite plausible under \(H_0\), we don’t have enough evidence to reject it — which is not the same as proving \(H_0\) is true (just like failing to find evidence for a theory doesn’t prove the theory false).

title: 3.5 Hypothesis Testing
text:
3.5.3 The p-value
The p-value is the number that formalizes “how likely would a result this extreme be, if the null hypothesis were true?” More precisely:

The p-value is the probability of observing a sample result at least as extreme as the one you found, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

Suppose we run a small experiment: 10 children play a violent video game, another 10 play a non-violent one, and we measure heart rate afterwards.

set.seed(1)
violent     <- rnorm(10, mean = 85, sd = 8)
non_violent <- rnorm(10, mean = 78, sd = 8)

t.test(violent, non_violent)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  violent and non_violent
t = 1.8112, df = 16.469, p-value = 0.08839
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.017735 13.151460
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
 86.05762  79.99076 


The p-value in the output tells us: if there were truly no difference in heart rate between the two conditions in the population (\(H_0\)), how likely is it that we’d see a sample difference at least this large, just due to chance? A small p-value (conventionally, below \(\alpha = .05\)) is treated as sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis, and conclude that the groups likely do differ in the population.

What a p-value does not mean
p-values are among the most misinterpreted numbers in all of statistics, so it is worth being explicit about what they do not tell you:

A p-value is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true. \(p = .03\) does not mean “there’s a 3% chance the null hypothesis is correct”. It’s a statement about how surprising the data would be if \(H_0\) were true — not a statement about how probable \(H_0\) itself is.
A p-value is not the probability that your result is due to chance. This sounds similar to the correct definition but subtly reverses the conditioning: the p-value assumes \(H_0\) is true from the start, it doesn’t tell you the probability of that assumption.
A small p-value does not mean the effect is large or important. As you saw in Effects, a p-value tells you how sure you can be that an effect isn’t exactly zero — not how big that effect is. A tiny, practically irrelevant effect can produce a very small p-value if the sample is large enough.
A non-significant result (\(p > .05\)) does not prove \(H_0\) is true. “We found no significant effect” means the data didn’t give us enough evidence to reject \(H_0\) — it does not mean we’ve shown there is truly no effect. The effect might be real but small, or the sample might simply be too small to detect it (see Power Analysis).

title: 3.5 Hypothesis Testing
text:
3.5.4 Confidence intervals
A p-value only gives a yes/no answer about whether an effect differs from zero. A confidence interval (CI) gives you more information: a plausible range of values for the true population effect, given your sample.
Look again at the t.test() output above — it reports a 95% confidence interval for the difference in means. The intuitive (if slightly informal) way to read this is: if we were to repeat this study many times, about 95% of the confidence intervals we’d compute this way would contain the true population difference. A narrower interval reflects a more precise estimate (usually from a larger sample, as you saw in Probability & Sampling); a wider one reflects more uncertainty.
As a quick rule of thumb that connects CIs back to p-values: if a 95% confidence interval for a mean difference (or a correlation, or a regression coefficient) does not contain zero, the result will also be statistically significant at \(\alpha = .05\) — the two tools are two views of the same underlying logic. The confidence interval has the advantage of also showing you the plausible size of the effect, not just whether it differs from zero.

title: 3.3 Covariance & Correlation
text:
You arrive here from Means & Variance, so you can already describe a single variable with its mean and variance. Here you’ll learn covariance and correlation: ways to describe how two variables move together, and why correlation is the standardized, easier-to-interpret version of covariance. Most research questions in communication science are ultimately about relationships between variables, and this is the simplest way to quantify one — it comes back in regression, scale construction, and factor analysis.
→ See this module in the skill tree

title: 3.3 Covariance & Correlation
section: 3.3.1 The difference between covariance and correlation
text:
3.3.1 The difference between covariance and correlation
If we look at the plots above, we see that the covariance and correlation are closely related. The difference is that the correlation is standardized, while the covariance is not. This means that:

The covariance can be any number, while the correlation is always between -1 and 1.
The covariance depends on the scale of the variables.

By the scale we mean the units in which the variables are measured. For instance, we can measure social media use in hours or in minutes per day. This shouldn’t change the relation between social media use and feelings of loneliness, but it does change the covariance.
To illustrate this, let’s plot the positive correlation scenario from above three times:

once with the X variable (social media use) in hours
once with the X variable in minutes
once with both the X and Y variables standardized (i.e, turn them into z-scores).










As we can see, the direction and strength of the relation is the same in all three plots. The only thing that changed is the scale of the variables, which you can see in the X and Y axis. This doesn’t affect the correlation (\(r = 0.508\) in all three cases), but it does affect the covariance:

For the original data, the covariance is \(1.099\), as we saw before
For the data where we increased the scale of X by a factor 60 (to go from hours to minutes), the covariance increased to \(65.931\).
In the final plot we standardized both the X and Y variables. As a result, the covariance is now identical to the correlation (\(r = 0.508, cov = 0.508\)). This is what we mean when we say that the correlation is the standardized version of the covariance!

title: 3.3 Covariance & Correlation
text:
3.3.2 Calculate covariance
The formula for the calculating the covariance between two variables \(X\) and \(Y\) in a sample1 is:
\[ cov(X, Y) = \frac{\sum (X_i - \bar{X}) (Y_i - \bar{Y})}{n-1} \]

\(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) are the individual values of \(X\) and \(Y\)
\(\bar{X}\) and \(\bar{Y}\) are the means of \(X\) and \(Y\)
\(n\) is the number of observations
\(\sum\) is the sum over all observations

Let’s perform this calculation in steps, to make it easier to follow. First, calculate the means for x and y.

d <- mutate(d, x_mean = mean(x),
               y_mean = mean(y))

Now calculate the deviation from the mean for both variables. This is the \(X_i - \bar{X}\) and \(Y_i - \bar{Y}\) part of the formula.

d <- mutate(d, x_deviation = x - x_mean,
               y_deviation = y - y_mean)

Then multiply these deviations.

d <- mutate(d, deviation_product = x_deviation * y_deviation)

Have a look at the intermediate results to see what we’ve done so far. Try to do the calculations in your head to see if you understand what’s going on.

d


  



Finally, sum the deviation products and divide by \(n-1\) to get the covariance. Here we use the sum() function to calculate the sum of the deviation_product column, and the nrow() function to get the number of observations in the data d.

dev_sum = sum(d$deviation_product)
n = nrow(d)
dev_sum / (n - 1)

[1] 22.5


Here we use the summarize function, which allows us to calculate summarizing statistics functions, such as sum() and n() (which gives the number of observations).
You can check your answer by using the cov() function, which is R’s built-in function for calculating the covariance.

cov(d$x, d$y)

[1] 22.5

title: 3.3 Covariance & Correlation
text:
3.3.3 Calculate correlation
The correlation is the standardized covariance. There are two ways to go about this:

First standardize the variables, then calculate the covariance
We can repeat the covariance calculation, but this time standardize the variables first. This is also what we showed in the previous section, where we plotted the data with the variables standardized.
To standardize a variable, we subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation (there is also the built in function scale() that can do this for you). Be carefull to use the parentheses correctly!

d <- mutate(d, x_z = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x),
               y_z = (y - mean(y)) / sd(y))

Now you can repeat the covariance calculation, but this time with the standardized variables x_z and y_z instead of x and y. Here we won’t repeat the steps, but instead use the built in cov() function with the standardized variables. We’ll also calculate the correlation of x and y using the cor() function, so that you can see that it works.

cov(d$x_z, d$y_z)

[1] 0.9

cor(d$x, d$y)

[1] 0.9




First calculate covariance, then standardize it
The other way to calculate the correlation is to first calculate the covariance, and then standardize it. For this we also need to know the variance of both x and y. Luckily, you already know how to calculate the variance, because this is the same as calculating the covariance of a variable with itself! We heartily invite you to try this yourself, but here we’ll just let R take care of the covariances for us. For this we again use the cov function, but this time we give it a tibble as input. R will then return the covariance matrix for all variables in the tibble.

d |>
  select(x, y) |>
  cov()

      x    y
x 250.0 22.5
y  22.5  2.5


Here we see four values:

The covariance of x with x (the variance of x), which is 250.
The covariance of y with y (the variance of y), which is 2.5.
The covariance of x with y, which we already know is 22.5.
The covariance of y with x, which is the same as the covariance of x with y, because the covariance is symmetric.

Given this information, the correlation between x and y can be calculated as:
\[ r = \frac{cov(X, Y)}{S_X S_Y} \]
Where \(S_X\) is the standard deviation of \(X\), which you get by taking the square root of the variance. \[ S_X = \sqrt{var(X)} \]
So the calculation is:

cov_xy = 22.5
Sx = sqrt(250)
Sy = sqrt(2.5)

cov_xy / (Sx * Sy)

[1] 0.9


Which is the same as the correlation we calculated before!
Now that you can describe a relationship in your sample, the next question is whether it also exists in the population. You’ll learn how to test that in Testing Associations.

title: 3.1 Means & Variance
text:
You arrive here from Functions and Packages, so you can already compute things in R with vectors and functions. Here you’ll learn what the mean, variance, and standard deviation of a variable actually tell you, and how to compute them, by hand once and then with mean(), var(), and sd(). This matters because nearly every statistic you’ll meet later in the book — t-tests, correlations, regression coefficients — is built on top of these two numbers.
→ See this module in the skill tree

title: 3.1 Means & Variance
text:
3.1.1 The mean: a balance point
Suppose we asked 10 respondents to rate their political interest on a scale from 1 (not interested at all) to 10 (very interested):

library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

political_interest <- c(2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9)

The mean is the number you already know as “the average”: add up all the values, and divide by how many there are.
\[ \bar{X} = \frac{\sum X_i}{n} \]

sum(political_interest) / length(political_interest)

[1] 5.2


Of course, R has a built-in function for this, so you’ll never actually need to type out the formula:

mean(political_interest)

[1] 5.2


It helps to think of the mean as a balance point. If you drew the 10 scores as weights on a see-saw, the mean is the point where the see-saw would balance. Some respondents are far below the mean, some are far above it, and the positive and negative distances exactly cancel out.
This “distance from the mean” is called a deviation, and it’s the building block for everything else in this chapter. For a given value \(X_i\), the deviation is \(X_i - \bar{X}\).

d <- tibble(political_interest) |>
  mutate(deviation = political_interest - mean(political_interest))

d


  



If you sum the deviation column, you’ll always get (approximately) zero — that’s exactly what “balance point” means.

sum(d$deviation)

[1] -1.776357e-15

title: 3.1 Means & Variance
section: 3.1.2 Variance and standard deviation: how spread out is the data?
text:
3.1.2 Variance and standard deviation: how spread out is the data?
The mean tells you where the center of the data is, but it tells you nothing about how spread out the scores are. Two samples can have the exact same mean while looking completely different: in one, everyone agrees and clusters close to the average; in the other, respondents are scattered from one extreme to the other. For a researcher, that difference matters a lot — a highly polarized sample is a different story than a uniformly moderate one.
To measure spread, we’d like to average the deviations from the mean. But as we just saw, the deviations always sum to (about) zero, so a plain average of them is useless — positive and negative deviations cancel out. The fix is to square each deviation first. Squaring makes every value positive, and it also makes large deviations count disproportionately more than small ones, which is a reasonable way to penalize scores that are far from the average.
That gives us the variance: the (roughly) average squared deviation from the mean.
\[ var(X) = \frac{\sum (X_i - \bar{X})^2}{n - 1} \]

d <- d |> mutate(squared_deviation = deviation^2)
d


  


sum(d$squared_deviation) / (length(political_interest) - 1)

[1] 5.288889


Again, R has a built-in function so you don’t need to do this by hand in practice:

var(political_interest)

[1] 5.288889



Why divide by \(n - 1\) and not \(n\)?
You might expect we’d divide by \(n\), the number of observations, since variance is supposed to be an average squared deviation. The reason we divide by \(n - 1\) instead is a subtle but important one: we’re almost always using a sample to estimate the variance of a population, and the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is, by construction, the value that makes the squared deviations in this particular sample as small as possible. That means a sample will systematically underestimate the true population variance just a little bit, on average. Dividing by the slightly smaller number \(n - 1\) instead of \(n\) corrects for this bias.
You don’t need to be able to re-derive this to use it correctly — just remember the rule of thumb: when you’re working with a sample (which is almost always the case in practice), use \(n - 1\). R’s var() and sd() functions already do this for you.


Standard deviation: back to the original units
One awkward thing about variance is that it’s expressed in squared units. If political interest is measured on a 1–10 scale, the variance is in “scale points squared”, which is hard to interpret intuitively. The standard deviation fixes this by taking the square root of the variance, bringing it back to the original scale:
\[ SD(X) = \sqrt{var(X)} \]

sqrt(var(political_interest))

[1] 2.299758

sd(political_interest)

[1] 2.299758


A useful (rough) intuition for the standard deviation: for many variables, most observations fall within about one SD of the mean, and nearly all fall within two or three SDs. So if political interest has a mean of 5.2 and an SD of 2.2, a respondent scoring 9 is unusually interested compared to the rest of the sample, while someone scoring 6 is close to typical.

title: 3.1 Means & Variance
section: 3.1.3 Why this matters for everything that follows
text:
3.1.3 Why this matters for everything that follows
The mean and the variance (or SD) aren’t just descriptive trivia — they are the two ingredients that almost every statistical test in this book combines in some way:

A t-test (in Comparing two Groups) compares the difference between two means, relative to how much variance there is within each group.
A correlation (in Correlation & Covariance) is built from deviations from the mean of two variables at once.
A regression model (in Multiple Regression) tries to explain variance in your outcome variable using one or more predictors.
Effect sizes (in Effects), like Cohen’s \(d\), are literally mean differences expressed in standard deviation units.

In other words: once you understand the mean as “where the center is” and the variance/SD as “how much do individual scores typically deviate from that center”, you already understand the core building block of most of the statistics you’ll see from here on.

title: 2.4 Pivoting and joining
text:
You arrive here from Grouping and summarizing, so you can already group and summarise data frames. Here you’ll reshape data between wide and long format with pivot_longer() and pivot_wider(), and combine separate data frames with the *_join() family. Survey, experiment, and platform data rarely arrive in exactly the shape you need, and long format is also required for many plots and models.
→ See this module in the skill tree

title: 2.4 Pivoting and joining
text:
2.4.1 Wide vs. long data
As a small toy example, consider a trust-in-news-media survey where three respondents were asked the same question at three points in time (t1, t2, t3):

library(tidyverse)

survey_wide <- tibble(
  id = 1:3,
  trust_t1 = c(5, 6, 4),
  trust_t2 = c(6, 6, 5),
  trust_t3 = c(7, 5, 6)
)
survey_wide


  



This is called wide format: each respondent is one row, and each measurement occasion gets its own column (trust_t1, trust_t2, trust_t3). Wide format is often how data is entered or exported (e.g. from Qualtrics), and it’s easy to read by eye. But it’s inconvenient for analysis: if you want to plot trust over time, or run a repeated-measures model, most R functions expect one row per observation rather than one row per respondent.
The alternative is long format, where every single measurement gets its own row:

survey_long <- survey_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("trust"), names_to = "wave", values_to = "trust")
survey_long


  



Now there are three rows per respondent (one per wave) instead of one row with three columns. This is the “tidy data” idea you’ll keep running into: each variable is a column, each observation is a row. Whether wide or long is “tidy” depends on what you call a variable — here, wave and trust are both meaningful variables in their own right, so the long format is the tidy one.

title: 2.4 Pivoting and joining
2.4 Pivoting and joining
text:
2.4.3 Pivoting wider: pivot_wider()
pivot_wider() does the opposite: it spreads one column’s distinct values out into multiple columns. This is useful when you need wide format for a specific function or for a readable table to report. It needs two arguments: names_from (which column’s values become the new column names) and values_from (which column’s values fill them in):

survey_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = wave, values_from = trust)


  



This recovers the original wide data frame. pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() are mirror images of each other — if you get stuck in one direction, it can help to picture the matching call in the other direction.

title: 2.4 Pivoting and joining
text:
2.4.4 Combining data frames: joins
Pivoting reshapes one data frame. Just as often, the information you need is split across multiple data frames, and you need to combine them. For example, suppose you also have a separate data frame about the media outlets each respondent follows most:

respondents <- tibble(
  id = 1:4,
  age = c(24, 31, 45, 19),
  favorite_outlet = c("nos", "telegraaf", "nos", "rtl")
)

outlets <- tibble(
  outlet_id = c("nos", "telegraaf", "volkskrant"),
  outlet_name = c("NOS", "De Telegraaf", "De Volkskrant"),
  outlet_type = c("public", "private", "private")
)

Here, respondents has one row per person, and outlets has one row per media outlet, with its own set of columns. To combine them, we need a key: a column (or set of columns) that identifies matching rows across the two data frames. In this case, favorite_outlet in respondents and outlet_id in outlets play that role, even though they have different names.

left_join()
left_join() keeps every row of the first (“left”) data frame, and adds columns from the second data frame wherever a match is found. When by = names differ between the two data frames, you write by = c("left_column" = "right_column"):

respondents |>
  left_join(outlets, by = c("favorite_outlet" = "outlet_id"))


  



Respondent 4 follows rtl, which doesn’t appear in outlets — so their outlet_name and outlet_type become NA, but the respondent’s row is still kept. This is the join to reach for by default whenever you want to enrich one data frame with extra information, without losing any of its original rows.


inner_join()
inner_join() keeps only the rows that have a match in both data frames:

respondents |>
  inner_join(outlets, by = c("favorite_outlet" = "outlet_id"))


  



Respondent 4 (favorite outlet rtl) disappears entirely, because there’s no matching row in outlets. Use inner_join() when a missing match means the row genuinely doesn’t belong in your analysis — for example, if you only want to analyse respondents whose outlet you have full information about.


full_join()
full_join() keeps every row from both data frames, matching where it can and filling in NA everywhere else:

respondents |>
  full_join(outlets, by = c("favorite_outlet" = "outlet_id"))


  



Now volkskrant also shows up as its own row, even though no respondent follows it, with NA for the respondent columns. This is useful when you want to see the complete picture from both sides, for instance to spot outlets that nobody in your sample follows.


Checking a join
Joins can silently go wrong in two ways, and it’s worth checking for both every time:

Unmatched rows: did more or fewer rows disappear (or gain NAs) than you expected? Compare nrow() before and after the join, and inspect any new NAs with filter(is.na(...)).
Duplicated keys: if a key value occurs more than once in the second data frame, each matching row in the first data frame gets duplicated once per match. For example, if outlets accidentally had two rows for "nos", every respondent who follows NOS would appear twice after the join. Always check count() on your join key in the second data frame first (outlets |> count(outlet_id)) to make sure each key is unique before joining.


outlets |> count(outlet_id)


  



Here every outlet_id occurs exactly once, so we know the join above won’t have silently duplicated any respondents.

1.6 Functions and Packages
text:
You arrive here from Data in R, so you can already work with data frames, extract columns, and recognize the common types of data they contain. Here you’ll learn how functions let you do* something with that data, and how packages give you access to thousands of ready-made functions beyond what R ships with by default. You’ll also pick up a few essential tricks for working with functions and packages without having to memorize everything by heart. Together, functions and packages are the toolbox you’ll reach for in every module from here on.*
→ See this module in the skill tree

title: 1.6 Functions and Packages
text:
1.6.1 Functions

What is a function?
99% of what you do in R will involve using functions. A function in R is like a mini-program that you can use to perform specific tasks. It takes input, processes it, and gives you an output. For example, there are functions for:

importing data
computing descriptive statistics
performing statistical tests
visualizing data

A function in R has the form:

output <- function_name(argument1, argument2, ...)`


function_name is a name to indicate which function you want to use. It is followed by parentheses.
arguments are the input of the function, and are inserted within the parentheses.
output is anything that is returned by the function.

For example, the function c combines multiple values into a vector.

x = c(1,2,3,4)

Now, we can use the mean function to calculate the mean of these numbers:

m <- mean(x)

The calculated mean, 2.5, is now assigned to the name m:

m

[1] 2.5



Optional arguments
In the c and mean functions above, all the arguments were required. To combine numbers into a vector, we needed to provide a list of numbers. To calculate a mean, we needed to provide a numeric vector.
In addition to the required arguments, a function can also have optional arguments, that give you more control over what a function does. For example, suppose we have a range of numbers that also contains a missing value. In R a missing value is called NA, which stands for Not Available:

x_with_missing <- c(1, 2, 3, NA, 4)

Now, if we call the mean function, R will say that the mean is unknown, since the third value is unknown:

mean(x_with_missing)

[1] NA


This is statistically a very correct answer. But often, if some values happen to be missing in your data, you want to be able to calculate the mean just for the numbers that are not missing. Fortunately, the mean function has an optional argument na.rm (remove NAs) that you can set to TRUE (or to T, which is short for TRUE) to ignore the NAs:

mean(x, na.rm=TRUE)

[1] 2.5


Notice that for the required argument, we directly provide the input x, but for the optional argument we include the argument name na.rm = TRUE. The reason is simply that there are other optional arguments, so we need to specify which one we’re using. (We’ll come back to how you can look up which optional arguments a function has below, in Working with functions and packages without memorizing everything.)


Using the pipe syntax
There is another common way to use functions in R using the pipe syntax. With the pipe syntax, you can pipe the first argument into the function, instead of putting it inside the parentheses. As you will see below, this allows you to create a pipeline of functions, which is often easier to read. 

argument1 |> function_name(argument2, ...)

For example, the following two lines of code give identical output:

mean(x_with_missing, na.rm=T)

[1] 2.5

x_with_missing |> mean(na.rm=T)

[1] 2.5


Notice how our first argument, the required argument x_with_missing, is piped into the mean function. Inside the mean function, we only specify the second argument, the optional argument na.rm.
So why do we need this alternative way of doing the same thing? The reason is that when writing code, you shouldn’t just think about what the code does, but also about how easy the code is to read. This not only helps you prevent mistakes, but also makes your analysis transparent. As you’ll see later, you’ll encounter many cases where your analysis requires you to string together multiple functions. In these cases, pipes make your code much easier to read.
For example, imagine we would want to round the result (2.5) up to a round number (3). With the pipe syntax we can just add the round function to our pipeline.

x_with_missing |>
  mean(na.rm=T) |>
  round()

You’ll see how powerful this can be later on, especially in the Data Management chapter. In order to prepare and clean up your data, you’ll often need to perform a series of functions in a specific order. The pipe syntax allows you to do this in a very readable way.

title: 1.6 Functions and Packages
text:
1.6.2 Packages

What is a package?
In R, a package is a collection of functions, data, and documentation that extends the capabilities of R. You can think of packages kind of like apps on your phone: they provide additional functionality that you can use to perform specific tasks. Also, like apps, you can install and uninstall packages as needed, directly from within R.
There are thousands of R packages available, which enables you to use almost any existing data analysis technique. R is not just a tool for statistical analysis, but also for data visualization, data collection, articifial intelligence, and much more. If there is anything you need to do, there is a good chance that someone has already written a package for it.


How to install
To use a package, you first need to install it. Installing a package only needs to be done once per system (unless you need to update it).

1. Install a package
Most packages are available on the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN), which is the main repository for R packages. To install these packages, all you need to know is their name.
For example, there is a package called lubridate that makes it easier to work with dates and times in your data. To install this package, you can use the install.packages() function:

install.packages("lubridate")







WarningWhat if R asks tot ‘install from source’?





When running install.packages() You sometimes get the message that There is a binary version available but the source version is later (we’re mainly seen this on Mac). You then get the question whether you want to install from source the package which needs compilation (Yes/no). To answer this question, you have to type “yes” or “no” in your R console.
It is then usually best to say NO. This will install a slightly older version of the package, but it will be much faster and easier to install. You often don’t need the latest version, so it’s not worth the extra hassle.
In case you’re curious, the reason for this is that the newest version has not been prepared for your system yet. They do have the source code, but it has not yet been compiled into a binary version that is ready to use. Think of the source code as a recipe, and the binary version as the ready-made dish. If you really want to have the newest version you can say “yes”, but you’ll have to cook it yourself! The main problem is that you will often need to install some extra software to do this, which can be a hassle. So unless you really need the newest version, it’s usually best to say “no”, and just install the older version that has already been prepared for your system.





2. Load a package
Once you have installed a package, it is not yet loaded into your current R session. Similar to when you install a new app on your phone, you need to open it every time you want to use it.
To use a package in your current R session, you can load it with the library() function:

library(lubridate)




Package documentation
Most packages come with good documentation that explains how to use the functions in the package. For individual functions you can use the ? operator to open the help page for that function, as we explain below. But there is often also a more general documentation that explains the package as a whole. This is called a vignette, and if a package has one, you can open it with the vignette() function.

vignette("lubridate")

You can look up vignettes and function documentation online. This is also a good way to find new packages for whatever you’re trying to do.

title: 1.6 Functions and Packages
section: 1.6.3 Working with functions and packages without memorizing everything
text:
1.6.3 Working with functions and packages without memorizing everything
One of the things that new users in R can find overwhelming, is that they think they need to learn all functions (and all their arguments) by heart. This is not the case! Aside from a handful of functions that you will use all the time, you will often need to look up how to use a function, or run into a package that just won’t install. Rather than learning everything by heart, you need to learn some tricks for how to quickly look up information, and how to troubleshoot when things go wrong.

How to Use the ? Symbol
One of the most important tricks is to use the built-in help system in R. You can quickly access documentation for any function using the ? symbol. This is a powerful tool that can help you understand how to use functions, what arguments they require, and what they return.
To view the documentation for a specific function, you simply need to type ? followed by the function name. For example, if you want to learn more about the mean() function, you would type:

?mean

This will open the help page, often in the bottom right pane of RStudio.


How to read the help page
The help page for a function is divided into several sections. The most important sections are:

Description
A brief description of what the function does. For the mean() function, the description is: Generic Function for the (Arithmetic) Mean.
By generic function, they mean that the function can have multiple implementations. When you think of the mean, you are probably thinking of the mean of a vector of numbers.

x = c(1,2,3,4)
mean(x)

[1] 2.5


But you can do more! For example, you can also calculate the mean of a vector of Date values:

dates = as.Date(c("2021-01-01", "2021-01-03"))
mean(dates)

[1] "2021-01-02"




Usage
The syntax of the function, including all the arguments it takes. For example, the mean() function has the following usage:

mean(x, ...)

## Default S3 method:
mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...)

The first part tells you that the most basic way to use the function is to provide an argument called x. What x is, is explained in the arguments section that we discuss below.
The ... at the end means that the function can take additional arguments. This is because the mean function is a generic function. Depending on the type of input you provide (e.g., numbers, dates), some arguments might not be relevant.
The second part tells you that the default method for the mean function has two additional arguments in addition to x: trim, and na.rm. Note an important difference with the x argument: these arguments have default values (0 and FALSE, respectively). This means that these arguments are optional. If you don’t specify them, the function will use these default values.
For example, notice that the na.rm argument is set to FALSE by default. As we can see in the Arguments section, this means that the function will not remove missing values by default. (NA stands for Not Available, and is used in R to indicate missing values, so na.rm is short for remove NAs).

x_with_missing <- c(1, 2, 3, NA, 4)
mean(x_with_missing)

[1] NA


If we want to remove missing values, we can set na.rm to TRUE:

mean(x_with_missing, na.rm=TRUE)

[1] 2.5








NoteTo name or not to name your arguments





Notice how in the code above we specify the argument name na.rm = TRUE to indicate that we want to use this optional argument. For the x argument we don’t need to specify the argument name, because it’s the first argument and the function knows that the first argument is x. Generally speaking, if you don’t specify the argument name, R will assume that you are providing the arguments in the order that they are listed in the usage section. Let’s think a bit about when we should and should not use argument names!
You could decide to always use argument names:

mean(x=x_with_missing, na.rm=TRUE)

[1] 2.5


This is fine, and sometimes you might want to do this for sake of clarity. But it’s also often unnecessary. For the mean function, it is obvious that the first argument is the input over which you want to calculate the mean, so you don’t need to specify the argument name.
On the opposite end of the spectrum, you could decide to never use argument names:

mean(x_with_missing, 0, TRUE)

[1] 2.5


Here the three arguments follow the order in the usage section: x, trim, na.rm.
This has two obvious downsides:

It is not obvious what the 0 and TRUE arguments are. The reader might thus have to look up the function documentation.
We now also need to specify the trim argument, because it comes before na.rm in the usage section.

So in general, it is often good to use argument names for optional arguments, like na.rm. For required arguments, like x, it is often not necessary. Arguably the best way to use the mean function with na.rm is therefore:

mean(x_with_missing, na.rm=TRUE)

[1] 2.5







Arguments
A description of all the arguments that the function takes. This should cover all the arguments that are listed in the usage section.
For example, the mean() function explains that the x argument is can be a numeric vector, but also something like a logical or date vector. For the na.rm argument it explains that if set to TRUE, missing values will be removed before calculating the mean.


Value
The value section explains what the function returns (i.e. the output).


Examples
The examples section shows you how to use the function. Honestly, this is often the most useful part of the help page. If you are not sure how to use a function, a great way to learn is to look at the examples. Usually, you can directly copy-paste these examples into your script and run them to see how the function works.



Using tab completion
A very usefull trick in RStudio, and in programming in general, is to use tab completion. The tab key on your keyboard (the one above the caps lock key) can be used to complete the name of a function or variable. And if there are multiple ways in which the name can be completed, R will show you all the options. (On some devices you might need to press Tab twice, or it might not work at all).
For example, type the following code in your R script:

mean()

Now place your cursor between the parentheses and press the Tab key. This should now list all the arguments for the mean function, including their descriptions!
Since the mean function is empty, you should only have seen the x argument (and the ... argument). But you can also use tab completion when adding additional arguments. Type the following code in your R script:

x = c(1,2,3,4)
mean(x, )

Now place your cursor between the parentheses after the comma, and press the Tab key. Now you should see the trim and na.rm arguments, because RStudio knows that these arguments apply to a mean function with a numeric input!
Tab completion works for file paths too, and not just for function arguments. If you use tab completion between quotes, RStudio will show you all the files in your working directory that match the characters you’ve typed so far. So you can use this inside functions like read_csv to quickly find the file you want to read.

library(tidyverse)
read_csv("")

Try it out! It can even help you find a file path you’ve half-forgotten, right from your R script.


Troubleshooting: what if a package won’t install?
Sometimes install.packages() fails, with an error that looks intimidating. A few things are worth trying, roughly in order:

Read the last few lines of the error, not the whole wall of text. It usually names the actual problem (e.g. a missing system library, or “package … is not available”).
Restart R (menu: Session -> Restart R) and try again. Half of all package problems are solved by a clean R session.
Update R and your packages. An outdated R version is a common cause of install failures, since packages increasingly require a recent R.
Try the pak package. pak is a modern, drop-in alternative to install.packages() that gives much clearer error messages and is often better at resolving tricky installs:


install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("lubridate")

If none of this works, don’t spend hours on it alone: copy the error message and ask your teacher or a classmate. Package installation issues are extremely common, and are rarely about something you did wrong.

title: 1.3 Reproducible Reports
text:
1.3.1 Integrating code and text
The classic way of working in R is to write your code in a script file. This is still a very common way of working, and it has many advantages. But today there are also great alternatives, that make it possible to integrate your code directly in your reporting.
In fact, the book that you are currently reading is written in one such alternatives, called Quarto. Quarto is a literate programming tool, which means that it allows you to write your code and your text in the same document. Any results and visualizations that you generate in your code can also be directly included in the output document. This is not only convenient, but also makes your analysis more transparent and reproducible. If you ever need to update your analysis, you can just rerun the code and the document will automatically update, including any tables, figures and statistial results that you generated.
And despite all those features, it really isn’t that different from writing an R script. In some ways it is even a more convenient way of working.
In some courses in this program, you will be asked to write your assignments in Quarto. This section therefore provides a brief introduction to working in Quarto.

Creating a Quarto file
You can create and work with Quarto directly in RStudio. For assignments, you will often be given a template Quarto file, but here we’ll create one from scratch. To create a new Quarto file in RStudio, go to the menu bar and select File > New File > Quarto document.
You’ll get a menu where you can select some options, such as whether you want the output to be created in HTML, PDF or Word. We’ll stick with the default HTML, because this doesn’t require any additional software to be installed. For now, the only thing you should change is the Title. Just name it something like My First Quarto Document, and click Create.
The new file will open in the editor, and you’ll see that it already contains some text and code, that also doubles as a quick tutorial. Roughly speaking, there are three general components.

1. The Header
At the top of the file there is a header, which is enclosed by three dashes ---. Here you can specify some general settings for the document, such as the title, the author, and the output format. The default is:

This means that the title of the document is “My First Quarto Document”, the output format is HTML, and the editor is the visual editor. You can add many more options to the header, but for now we’ll stick with the basics.






NoteVisual or Source editor





The Quarto editor can be source or visual. In visual mode, everything looks a bit more pretty. It doesn’t yet look as pretty as when you render the document (which we’ll show you in a bit), but it’s a bit easier to read. Also, in the toolbar you get some buttons to make text bold or italics, add codeblocks, insert images, create tables, etc.
In source mode, everything is just in plain text. Behind the scenes, Quarto uses a format called Markdown to format the text. Markdown is a type of markup language (like HTML). What this means is that any formatting that you do (e.g., bold, tables, lists) is done by writing the text in a specific way. For example, to make a word bold, you write it between two asterisks **like this**.
Working in source mode can be convenient if you’re already familiar with Markdown. If not, we recommend sticking with visual mode for now, and maybe forever.





2. The textual content
After the header, you can start writing your text. This works like a light version of Word. You can add heading, lists, tables, images, and more.


3. The code chunks
At some point you see a code chunk, which looks like:

{r}
1 + 1

Inside these code chunks you can write R code. When you render the document, the code will be executed, and the output will be shown in the document.
While working on the document you can also run the code chunks separately (i.e. without rendering). You can do this like you would do in an R script, by selectin the code you want to run and hitting Run (or Ctrl/Cmd + Enter). But there is also a convenient option to run the entire code chunk at once by clicking on the run current chunk button in the top right of the code chunk. Here you also find a button to run all the chunks above the current one.
To add a new block, you can click on the Insert button in the toolbar, and select Executable Cell -> R.



Rendering the document
When you’re done writing your document, or if you want to see a preview, you can render the document by clicking the Render button in the toolbar (or hitting Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K). Try it now! If you did not yet save your Quarto file, R will first ask you to save it. You should then give it a name with the .qmd (Quarto Markdown) extension, for example my-first-quarto-document.qmd. This should produce an HTML file that opens in your browser (unless you changed something and broke it).
There is one big challenge when working with Quarto, which is also a blessing in disguise. If there is ANY error in your code, the entire document will not render. This can be frustrating, especially if you need to hand in an assignment in a few minutes. So whenever you’re working with Quarty, make sure to frequently render your document while you’re working on it, to catch any errors early on. It is much easier to trace back an error if you only made a few changes since the last time you rendered the document. If you only render the document at the end, you might have to go through the entire document to find the error. (though the error messages will tell you where to look)
So why is this a blessing in disguise? It forces you to write your code in a way that is clean and well-structured. When working in an R script, a common mistake to make is that some pieces of code depend on code that is further down in the script. For example, if you use a certain column on line 10, but you only create that column on line 20. This might not pose a problem while you’re working on it, but it will bite you when for whatever reason you need to rerun the entire script. Quarto forces you to write your code in a way that if you run the entire script from scratch, it will work.


⚠️ Before you submit: use embed-resources: true






ImportantThis could cost you points if you forget it



When Quarto renders an HTML file, it does not put everything into that one .html file by default. Figures, plots, and other generated content are saved as separate files, in a folder next to your HTML file (usually named something like my-report_files/).
The HTML file just contains links to that folder. This means that if you only upload the .html file to Canvas — without that folder — your figures, images, and sometimes even your formatting will be missing when your teacher opens it, even though everything looked perfectly fine on your own computer!
The fix is to add one line to the header (the part between the --- at the top of your file), so that Quarto embeds everything directly into the single HTML file instead:
---
title: "My Report"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
---
Note that you need to copy the format and html lines as well — just adding embed-resources: true by itself won’t work. Also, make sure that html: and embed-resources is indented exactly like in the example above, with two spaces before html: and four spaces before embed-resources.


Once this option is set, every time you render, you get one single, self-contained .html file that you can safely upload anywhere — Canvas, email, a USB stick — and it will look exactly the same for whoever opens it, with no extra folder required.
How to tell whether it worked: after rendering, look in the folder next to your .qmd file.

Without embed-resources, you’ll see your .html file and a separate ..._files/ folder.
With embed-resources: true, you’ll only see the .html file — everything is already baked inside it. This is a quick, reliable way to check before you submit: if you still see a _files folder being created, double check your YAML header.

title: 1.3 Reproducible Reports
text:
1.3.2 Some tips and warnings

Turn on 'Render on save'
In the toolbar you can turn on Render on Save. This way, any time you save the document, it will try to render. Now make sure to save often (get used to using Ctrl/Cmd + s). This way you can catch any rendering errors early on.

The working directory is the folder where the Quarto file is located
A Quarto file will always use it’s own location as the working directory This is actually quite convenient. Just make sure to put your Quarto file in the same directory as your data, and you’re good to go.


Use code block parameters
You can add parameters to the code chunks. For example, the following code chunk will only show the code, but not the output:

{r, results=FALSE}
1 + 1

Following this same notation, you can set the following parameters:

{r, results=F}: show the code, but not the output
{r, eval=F}: show the code, but do not run it
{r, echo=F}: do not show the code, but show the output
{r, message=F}: do not show any messages that are generated by the code. This can for instance hide the message that is printed when you run library(tidyverse).
{r, warning=F}: do not show any warnings that are generated by the code. This is more dangerous than hiding messages, but if you are sure that the warning is harmless, you can use this to make the document cleaner.
{r, message=F, warning=F}: separate multiple parameters with a comma.
{r, cache=T}: cache the output. This way, if you render the document again, but the code chunk did not change, it will not rerun the code. If you have any code that takes a long time to run, this allows you to still render the document quickly (which is especially useful if you have Render on Save turned on). Just make sure to turn cache of before rendering the final version, to be sure that everything is up to date.

title: 1.1 Basic Computer Skills
text:
Basic computer skills are the foundation everything else in this book builds on. Most of you will already have plenty of experience using a computer, but there can still be gaps in your understanding, especially around things like how the file system actually works. This chapter gives a quick overview of the key skills worth having. We highly recommend reading through it once to see where you stand.

title: 1.1 Basic Computer Skills
text:
1.1.1 Files and folders
Everything on your computer — documents, photos, programs, and (soon) your data files — is stored as a file, and files are organised into folders (also called directories). This is called the file system, and most people navigate it using a file explorer. The following example is for MacOS, but it works the same on Windows and Linux.





You might already have a good intuition for how to use a file explorer. However, to effectively work with data, and responsibly handle sensitive information, you need a good understand how files and folders are stored on your computer, and develop good habits for keeping your file system organised.

The File System
The structure of the file system is referred to as a tree. Starting with a root folder at the top, it branches downward into subfolders, which can contain more subfolders, and so on. Here is a tree representation of the same file system shown in the file explorer above.

The most important thing to understand is that every file has a unique location in the file system. So while there are two files called survey_data.csv in the example above, they are not the same file! This has two important implications for data management.

Firstly, you need to understand how your computer refers to unique files and folders by their path. This enables you to write analysis scripts that can read and write files without relying on the file explorer, which improves reproducibility and makes it easier to work in teams. We cover this in the next section.
Secondly, you need to organise your files system properly, so that you don’t lose track of where data is stored. This is especially important when working with sensitive data, which comes with legal and ethical responsibilities to keep it safe and delete it when you’re done with it. In our example above, we show a common, sloppy procedure: someone downloads survey_data.csv into their Downloads folder, and then copies it into their project folder. This leaves a useless copy of sensitive data in the Downloads folder, where it’s likely to be forgotten and left there indefinitely.



Absolute file paths
The two versions of survey_data.csv above are in different locations, and your computer needs to know which one you mean when you refer to it. To uniquely identify these files, you can specify their asbolute path: the chain of folders you need to follow from the root of the tree to that file. The two files above have the following paths:
/Users/Chris/Projects/master_thesis/survey_data.csv
/Users/Chris/Downloads/data/survey_data.csv
In Windows this works the same way, but the slashes are reversed and the root of the tree is a drive letter:
C:\Users\Chris\Projects\master_thesis\survey_data.csv
C:\Users\Chris\Downloads\data\survey_data.csv






NoteHow do I find a file’s absolute path?





You can use your file explorer to find a file’s absolute path, and copy it into your analysis script.

macOS (Finder): select the file, then press Cmd + Option + C to copy its path, or right-click while holding Option for a “Copy as Pathname” option.
Windows (File Explorer): hold Shift and right-click the file, then choose “Copy as path”.

We’ll also show a couple of handy RStudio-specific tricks for this later in the book.



An absolute path specifies the EXACT location of the file. However, this has two drawbacks:

It’s long to type, and easy to get wrong.
It’s tied to one specific computer and user. If our example user Chris sends their analysis script to a colleague, the absolute path C:\Users\Chris\Projects\master_thesis\survey_data.csv will not exist on the colleague’s computer, and the script will fail.

This is why you should almost always use relative paths instead of absolute ones.


Relative paths and working directories
A relative path describes a file’s location relative to the current working directory. For example, if the working directory is /Users/Chris/Projects, the relative path to survey_data.csv is:
master_thesis/survey_data.csv
To see how this works, scroll up to the tree diagram and imagine that your computer is “standing” in the Projects folder. From there, you simply follow the chain of folders down to the file you want.
Analysis software like R allows you make any folder the working directory. We’ll show you how to do this later when we introduce RStudio, which makes this very easy. The general recommendation is to set the working directory to the folder of a project you’re working in, like /Users/Chris/Projects/master_thesis. This has two great benefits:

You can directly read and write files in that project folder, using only the file name.
You can move the whole project folder to a different computer. Since the paths are relative to that folder, all the scripts will still work. This is great for reproducibility and collaboration.

text:
1.1.2 File types and extensions
The short suffix after the dot in a file name — the file extension — tells your computer (and you) what kind of file it is, and which program should open it. Many file explorers hide extensions by default; it’s worth turning this setting on, since in this course the difference between file types genuinely matters.
Some of the extensions you’ll run into most often in this book:







Extension
What it is




.csv
Comma-separated values: a plain-text table, one row per line, values separated by commas. The most common format for exchanging data.


.xlsx / .xls
An Excel spreadsheet (a “workbook”). Looks similar to a .csv when opened, but is stored in a more complex, non-plain-text format that can also hold formulas, formatting, and multiple sheets.


.txt
A plain-text file: just characters, no formatting.


.r / .R
An R script: plain text containing R code.


.json
A structured, plain-text format often used to exchange data between programs (you’ll encounter this if you ever work with APIs).


.pdf
A fixed-layout document, for reading, not editing.


.docx
A Microsoft Word document.


.zip
A compressed archive bundling multiple files together — covered next.

title: 1.1 Basic Computer Skills
text:
1.1.3 Zip files
A zip file (extension .zip) is an archive: a single file that contains, and compresses, a whole bundle of other files and folders. Zip files are everywhere once you start downloading course materials or datasets, for two reasons: they let you download many files in one go, and compression makes the download smaller.
The reasons we single them out here, is that you need to know how to handle them properly. A common mistake is that people double click it like a normal folder. This will show you the contents, but the files inside are still “inside” the zip file, and most programs won’t be able to read them until you extract (or “unzip”) them.
On both Windows and macOS, this is usually as simple as right-clicking the .zip file and choosing “Extract All…” or “Extract”. Depending on what you choose, it either need to specify where to extract the files to, or it will extract them to the same folder as the zip file itself.
An example of this is shown in the file tree above. Inside the Downloads folder, there is a zip file called data.zip, and the data folder represents the contents of that zip file after extraction. This also reveals another data sensitivity pitfall: if the survey_data.csv file came out of the zip file, it means that it’s now actually stored in three places: the data.zip file, the extracted data folder, and the copy in the master_thesis folder.

title: Data Literacy
text:
Research methods are a critical foundation of the social sciences. They are the key to building reliable knowledge about how people, organizations, and societies work. Whenever we want to move beyond gut feelings and assumptions—whether to understand complex social problems, build convincing arguments, or make effective decisions—research methods provide the critical tools we need to gather evidence and test our ideas against reality.
Learning how to do research can be a lot of fun. It is exciting to see how data can be used to answer questions about the world, and it is satisfying to learn how to design a study, collect data, and run analyses yourself. But it also requires dedication. Over the course of several years, you will gradually build up your knowledge and skills. And at times, you will feel frustrated, confused, or even overwhelmed. That’s the price of learning hard things, and it is a price worth paying.
However, you might be wondering: is all that effort also worth it for me personally? You might be here to build a career in public policy, journalism, communication, or consultancy, or to more effectively fight for causes you believe in. If you are not planning to become a researcher, why do you need to learn how to design studies, collect data, and run analyses?
The answer is that studying how to properly do research is about so much more than being a researcher. You are not just learning tricks you can use to collect data and run analyses. You learn how to think critically about how data can be used and misused to tell stories. In short, you are learning how to be data literate. And the most effective way to train this literacy, is to speak, read, and write the language of data yourself.
Data literacy is essential in today’s data-driven society. Whether you go on to work in academia, step into a professional role in government, media, or business, or simply navigate the news and debates in your personal life, you are constantly surrounded by data. Claims in science, politics, organizations, and everyday media are routinely justified with numbers, graphs, and analyses. To function effectively as a professional, a scholar, and an informed citizen, you need to understand how data is used to build arguments, and where that process can go wrong.

text:
2. What Is Data Literacy?
Data literacy is the ability to understand, construct, and evaluate the relationship between data and stories.
When scientists, organizations, governments, or citizens act, they do not act on raw spreadsheets. Data by itself does not tell you what to do. People act on stories: narratives about what is happening in the world, how people behave, what caused a problem, or what the consequences of an intervention will be.
In academia, professional life, and public debate, these stories are rarely accepted on their own. They need to be backed up by empirical evidence—by data.





flowchart LR
    subgraph DataCol ["Data"]
        D1["Observations & Measurements"]
        D2["Survey Results"]
        D3["Digital Trace Data"]
    end

    subgraph StoryCol ["Stories"]
        S1["How a problem works"]
        S2["How people will behave"]
        S3["Expected consequences"]
    end

    D1 --> S1
    D2 --> S2
    D3 --> S3






Every research method you learn in this program—whether it is phrasing a survey question, sampling respondents, running a regression, or training a text classifier—is about how we draw the arrows between the data column on the left and the story column on the right.

title: Data Literacy
section: 3. Four Perspectives on Data and Stories
text:
3. Four Perspectives on Data and Stories
If we think of methods courses only as training for “the researcher,” it is easy to miss how broadly relevant these skills are. In practice, there are four different ways you can look at the relationship between data and stories.
We call these the four perspectives of data literacy: 1. The Strategic perspective 2. The Advocacy perspective 3. The Critical perspective 4. The Research perspective
Across all four perspectives, we look at the exact same two columns: Data and Stories. The difference is where the question mark is—what problem are you trying to solve?


1. The Strategic Perspective: Weighing Stories to Make a Choice
From the strategic perspective, you have to make a decision—often a simple yes or no, and often without the time or budget to collect new data.
Around any major choice, you are confronted with multiple stories backed by different kinds of existing data—for example, a story about public health, a story about human behavior, and a story about mental well-being. Multiple distinct stories can point toward the same “yes” decision, while other stories point toward “no.” Your task is to compare and weigh these stories against each other to decide which ones should guide your choice.

The core task: Using existing data to compare and weigh different stories in order to make a decision.
Where the question mark is: On the stories—which of these data-backed stories are strong enough and important enough to base our decision on?






flowchart LR
    subgraph DataCol ["Existing Data"]
        D1["Data source 1"]
        D2["Data source 2"]
        D3["Data source 3"]
    end

    subgraph StoryCol ["Competing Stories"]
        S1["<b>?</b> Story A (Yes)"]
        S2["<b>?</b> Story B (Yes)"]
        S3["<b>?</b> Story C (No)"]
    end

    D1 --> S1
    D2 --> S2
    D2 --> S3
    D3 --> S3

    classDef question fill:#e8f8f5,stroke:#18bc9c,stroke-width:2px
    class S1,S2,S3 question






When you work in management, policy advice, research leadership, or strategy—or when you have to make an informed choice in your own life based on competing evidence—this is your main perspective. You have to look at the available evidence behind each story, decide how much weight each story deserves, and commit to a course of action.



2. The Advocacy Perspective: Defending or Challenging a Story
Sometimes the decision has already been made, or you are representing a specific cause, organization, or theoretical position. Here, the story you want to tell is fixed: you want to convince others of a specific narrative (or dismantle a competing one).
From the advocacy perspective, your goal is to use data to make a convincing case for that story, often by comparing it favorably to alternative stories.

The core task: Selecting, framing, and connecting data to argue for (or against) a specific story.
Where the question mark is: On the arrows connecting multiple data sources to the stories—how do we connect the available data to build the strongest case for our story?

        D1["Data source 1"]
        D2["Data source 2"]
        D3["Data source 3"]
    end

        S1["Chosen Story"]
        S2["Competing Story"]
    end

    D2 == "<b>?</b>" ==> S1

    linkStyle 1 stroke:#18bc9c,stroke-width:2px;
    linkStyle 2 stroke:#95a5a6,stroke-dasharray: 5 5;






You use this perspective in communication, campaigning, NGO advocacy, politics, consultancy, or when arguing for the societal relevance of a research project. To advocate a position effectively and responsibly, you need to understand which data points genuinely support your story, how they compare to competing narratives, and how to present them clearly without making false claims.



3. The Critical Perspective: Evaluating a Story
From the critical perspective, someone else presents you with a story and claims that it is supported by data. Your task is not to sell the story or make the initial policy choice, but to evaluate whether the story actually holds up against the evidence.

The core task: Assessing how well a given story is corroborated by the data, and asking which other data or stories are being left out.
Where the question mark is: On the validity of the connection between the data and the presented story.






flowchart LR
    subgraph DataCol ["Data"]
        D1["Presented Data"]
        D2["Ignored / Missing Data"]
    end

    subgraph StoryCol ["Story"]
        S1["Presented Story"]
    end

    D1 -- "<b>?</b> Valid link?" --> S1
    D2 -. "<b>?</b> Why left out?" .-> S1

    linkStyle 0 stroke:#e67e22,stroke-width:2px;
    linkStyle 1 stroke:#95a5a6,stroke-dasharray: 5 5;






This is the classic perspective of a scientist conducting peer review, a journalist checking claims, an auditor, or an inquiry committee—as well as your own perspective in daily life whenever you critically read the news or evaluate claims on social media. When an organization, government, or study claims a conclusion is inevitable based on “the numbers,” the critical perspective asks whether the data is reliable, whether the interpretation makes sense, and how other relevant data was weighed or ignored.



4. The Research Perspective: Creating the Data
Finally, there is the research perspective. Often we realize that we cannot properly weigh, defend, or evaluate a story because we simply do not have the right evidence yet. We need new or better data to find out if a story is actually true.

The core task: Designing and executing data collection and analysis to corroborate or test stories.
Where the question mark is: On the data node itself—what data do we need, and how do we create it reliably?

title: Data Literacy
section: 4. One Case, Four Perspectives: The Nighttime Curfew
text:
4. One Case, Four Perspectives: The Nighttime Curfew
To see how these four perspectives come together in practice—and why social science is central to all of them—consider the decision to introduce a nighttime curfew (avondklok) during the COVID-19 pandemic.
At first glance, a pandemic measure might seem like a purely medical or epidemiological issue. In reality, a curfew is entirely about social science: * Human behavior: A curfew only reduces infections if people actually change their behavior. Will citizens comply, or will they visit friends earlier in the day, stay the night, or lose trust in authorities? * Mental health and social well-being: Restricting movement has direct psychological consequences, such as loneliness and stress, especially among young people. * Democratic values and legitimacy: A curfew restricts fundamental freedoms. How do we weigh public health gains against democratic norms and social cohesion?
Around this single decision (“Do we introduce the curfew: yes or no?”), there are several distinct stories—a story about viral transmission, a story about behavioral compliance, a story about youth mental health, and a story about fundamental rights. Now look at how different people approach this exact same situation from our four perspectives:

Strategic perspective (e.g., a politician or policy advisor): Has to decide yes or no on the curfew tonight. There is no time for new research. They have to look at existing data behind multiple stories—epidemiological models pointing to “yes,” behavioral surveys questioning compliance, and mental health warnings pointing to “no”—and decide how to weigh those stories against each other.
Advocacy perspective (e.g., a government spokesperson or an interest group): Once the government decides “yes,” the spokesperson has to sell the story that the curfew is necessary and effective using the available data. Conversely, an advocacy group for youth welfare uses data on mental health to champion the competing story and challenge the government’s argument.
Critical perspective (e.g., a journalist, an academic peer reviewer, or a critical citizen): Listens to the press conference or reads the underlying reports and critically tests the government’s story against the data. How reliable are the model projections from other countries? And notice how the government’s story relies almost entirely on infection data, while data on psychological consequences and democratic support received very little weight.
Research perspective (e.g., university researchers, social scientists at the Netherlands Institute for Social Research (SCP), or a parliamentary inquiry committee): Looks at what is missing. What data did we lack when making this choice? How do we design a rigorous study now to measure the actual behavioral and psychological impact, so we can build scientific knowledge and make better decisions in the future?

Whenever you step into any of these perspectives, four fundamental questions help you navigate the link between data and stories: 1. What data do we have? 2. Which data are we looking at, and how are we weighing it? (Why does one story get priority while another—such as psychological impact—gets ignored?) 3. What data is missing? 4. How do we interpret the data, and how reliable is it?

title: Data Literacy
section: 5. How Your Curriculum Builds Data Literacy (And Why AI Cannot Think for You)
text:
5. How Your Curriculum Builds Data Literacy (And Why AI Cannot Think for You)
Throughout your study program, you will spend a lot of time working from the Research perspective. You will collect data yourself, clean it, write code, and run statistical analyses.
Again, the primary reason for this is not that we expect everyone to become a full-time academic researcher, although some of you will. Rather, practicing the research perspective is what gives you the intuition needed to master the other three perspectives.
It is very hard to evaluate how reliable a dataset is (Critical perspective), weigh conflicting stories before a big decision (Strategic perspective), or build a solid data-driven argument (Advocacy perspective) if you have never built a dataset or run an analysis yourself. When you only see finished graphs in a paper or policy report, data looks neat and objective. Once you have designed a survey, coded text, or run a regression model yourself, you develop an intuition for how many choices, assumptions, and limitations are hidden behind a single number.
This is also why learning research methods remains essential in an age of Artificial Intelligence. AI can perform data analysis, and when you use it responsibly, it is a powerful tool to help you learn and execute data analysis. What AI cannot do, however, is think for you. To use AI effectively without being misled by it, you need your own methodological intuition. More importantly, even when AI can point out in what ways a story is or is not supported by data, you have to understand what those limitations actually mean in context—and how to weigh them against a complex, holistic story that also involves normative perspectives, democratic values, and human emotion.
As you move through the methods curriculum, keep these four perspectives in mind: * In your early methods courses, you will focus on the building blocks: how data is created, measured, and analyzed (Research perspective). * As you progress—and especially in project courses later in your studies—you will increasingly apply this knowledge across all four perspectives: using existing data to weigh stories and advise on decisions (Strategic), defending or challenging a narrative with empirical evidence (Advocacy), and critically evaluating the data stories of others (Critical).
Every technical skill in the chapters that follow is a piece of that larger puzzle.
